Prognostic Discussion for 6 to 10 and 8 to 14 day outlooks
NWS Climate Prediction Center College Park, MD
300 PM EST Sat November 21 2026
6-10 DAY OUTLOOK FOR NOV 27 - DEC 01, 2026
The 500-hPa height field across North America and adjacent areas is in
transition during this period, and models are in fair agreement at best with
the placement of mean 500-hPa features and the day-to-day evolution of the
mid-level pattern. The ensemble means are in decent agreement at the start of
the period, showing a progressive pattern with a series of shortwaves passing
through the southern Contiguous United States (CONUS). Thereafter, the model
solutions begin to diverge in their depictions of the day-to-day changes in a
progressive, transitioning pattern that begins to settle down later week-2.
Models agree that the period begins with a moderately amplified 500-hPa ridge
over the western CONUS that pushes eastward and rapidly dissipates as a series
of shortwaves begin to move across the CONUS . The mid-level ridge dissipates as
it pushes eastward into a downstream mid-level trough centered over the
south-central or southeastern CONUS, quickly kicking it eastward into the
western Atlantic. The GEFS mean is slower to break down the positive 500-hPa
 anomalies initially over the western CONUS, and while the European ensemble
(ECENS) and Canadian ensemble (CMCE) means are in better agreement showing a
quicker evolution, the forecast leans more toward the GEFS, which is more
consistent with model runs from the past few days. To the north and west of the
CONUS, the period starts with a mid-level trough over the southern CONUS that
moves eastward as the upstream ridge pushes into the region and quickly
dissipates. Farther north and west, positive 500-hPa height anomalies are
expected to decline as the progressive, transitioning pattern becomes
established. By late in the period or during week-2, a less progressive pattern
evolves and positive mid-level height anomalies are established again across
Canada, but there is significant uncertainty in the day-to-day details of how
the height field evolves as the mid-level ridging across Canada is temporarily
broken up. Farther west, there is additional model disparity regarding the
evolution of an amplified mid-level trough initially over the central North
Pacific. As one or more shortwaves kick downstream into the CONUS from this
amplified trough, the amplified mid-level trough is temporarily disrupted
before reloading farther west. At the end of the period, the ECENS mean is
strongest with the reestablished trough centered over the Aleutians while the
CMCE develops a slightly weaker feature centered farther to the northwest. The
GEFS mean reestablishes the trough near the ECENS mean solution, but shows an
elongated area of subnormal 500-hPa heights that stretch well eastward into the
shortwave train evolving over the western and central CONUS . The other ensemble
means build a weak ridge between the North Pacific trough and the mid-level
shortwaves impacting the CONUS, albeit in different locations. Again, despite
the CMCE and ECENS means being more consistent with each other, the official
forecast leans towards the GEFS mean since it is most consistent with past
runs. However, the differences in model handling of this transitioning pattern
reduces confidence in the official forecast.
The differences in the way the various models depict the evolution of the
height pattern leads to differing temperature and precipitation output.
Uncertainty is additionally increased because in some areas there is a
significant discrepancy between the raw output, and the statistically-derived
reforecast and bias-corrected output. The official forecast is a blend of these
solutions (giving more weight to the GEFS) and the analog to the manual blend,
which is only in fair agreement with any of the other tools. However, the
mid-level ridge pushing eastward from the western CONUS is expected to favor
above-normal temperatures over much of the CONUS from the south-central Plains,
Middle Mississippi and Ohio Valleys, and Mid-Atlantic region to the north and
east. The best odds for warmer than normal conditions cover the extreme
north-central CONUS (over 70 percent) with a secondary maximum across southern
parts of California and Arizona. Farther south, across the Gulf Coast Region
and the Southeast, temperature guidance is inconsistent, but most tools favor
at least a relative minimum in mean temperature anomalies along the Gulf Coast.
Raw and bias-corrected tools are considerably colder than the reforecasts, but
given the mid-level trough expected there early in the period, with additional
shortwaves moving in from the west, the forecast favors the colder solution and
shows nominally-enhanced odds of colder than normal conditions along the Gulf
Coast, and near-normal mean temperatures from south Texas through the lower
Mid-Atlantic. Meanwhile, 500-hPa heights average above normal across Alaska,
favoring above-normal temperatures there. Hawaii, in contrast, is expected to
be under the influence of surface high pressure to the north and west which is
expected to result in subnormal temperatures, though uncertainty is introduced
by above-normal sea surface temperatures surrounding the island chain.
The shortwave(s) kicked eastward from the North Pacific trough favors
above-normal precipitation in the western and north-central CONUS . The best
odds for enhanced totals cover the central West Coast and western Great Basin,
where chances exceed 50 percent. The likelihood of surplus precipitation
decreases farther east as the shortwave deamplifies and its track becomes less
certain. Farther south and east, one or more surface storm systems are expected
to affect the Gulf and Atlantic Coast regions in association with the mid-level
 trough in that region, resulting in enhanced chances for above-normal
precipitation there. Chances for abnormal wetness are highest in the Florida
Peninsula (over 50 percent). Elsewhere, the uncertainty in the evolution of
mid-level features creates significant uncertainty across Alaska, but the
preponderance of tools slightly favor subnormal rainfall in the north and west
Mainland, with above-normal amounts slightly favored over south-central and
southeastern parts of the state. Over Hawaii, increased chances for
below-normal precipitation cover the western half of the island chain while
amounts are expected to be closer to normal over the eastern sections,
consistent with a preponderance of the tools.
The official 6-10 day 500-hPa height blend consists of 20% of Today's 0z GFS
Ensemble Mean centered on Day 8, 35% of Today's 6z GFS Ensemble Mean centered
on Day 8, 20% of Today's 0z European Ensemble Mean centered on Day 8, 10% of
Today's operational 0z ECMWF centered on Day 8, and 15% of Today's 0z Canadian
Ensemble Mean centered on Day 8
FORECAST CONFIDENCE FOR THE 6-10 DAY PERIOD: Below average, 2 out of 5, due to
model inconsistencies in the placement of mean 500-hPa height anomaly centers
in the North Pacific and southern Canada, along with differing mean 500-hPa
height anomalies in the southwestern CONUS . There are also differences between
the raw and the statistically-adjusted model temperature and precipitation
tools, and uncertainty inherent to a transitioning pattern.
8-14 DAY OUTLOOK FOR NOV 29 - DEC 05, 2026
The mid-level pattern settles down some during week-2, but there remains
significant model disparity in the handling of the 500-hPa height pattern as it
evolves into what appears to be a more stable regime. By the end of week-2,
models are in fair general agreement depicting a mid-level trough from the
North Pacific and adjacent Siberia eastward into the central North Pacific, and
one or two progressive shortwaves farther east impacting the CONUS . Model
solutions diverge on the specifics, however, with the ECENS and CMCE means
ending week-2 with a decent mid-level trough centered over the south-central or
southeastern CONUS, and some degree of mid-level ridging along the immediate
West Coast between the two mid-level troughs . The CMCE mean shows two
shortwaves affecting the CONUS, one centered over the Southeast or South
Atlantic Region and another entering the central West Coast approximately where
the other ensemble means place a weak ridge . Farther north, above-normal
 500-hPa heights are broadly established across much of northern North America
by the end of week-2, but there are significant model differences regarding how
this set-up evolves, and with the forecast location of the greatest 500-hPa
positive anomalies . These model differences result in differing temperature and
precipitation outputs, and additional uncertainties are introduced by continued
differences between the raw model output, the statistically-derived temperature
and precipitation forecasts, and the analog to the manual blend . A blend of
these tools was used in the official forecasts, with more weight given to the
GEFS mean (due to its greater consistency) and the analogs .
The resulting temperature forecast favors abnormally mild temperatures over a
large part of the CONUS, with the best chances across the Great Lakes and
Northeast, where positive 500-hPa height anomalies are most prevalent. Chances
for enhanced warmth exceed 60 percent in this region. Farther west, there is a
corridor of forecast near-normal temperatures extending from the central West
Coast through portions of the Southern Rockies and High Plains. Subnormal
 500-hPa mean heights and unsettled weather associated with one or more
shortwaves are expected to keep temperatures down, especially later in the
period. Above-normal mid-level heights prevail across Alaska, favoring
above-normal temperatures, while building 500-hPa heights and warmer than
normal sea surface temperatures favor a return of warmer than normal weather to
Hawaii.
Through at least the middle of week-2, one or more shortwaves traversing the
 CONUS favors increased precipitation across most of the CONUS, especially
across the southern tier of the country closest to the storm track, and across
the central Rockies and Great Plains in association with potential lee side
cyclogenesis. The likelihood of surplus precipitation exceeds 40 percent in
these areas. Near normal precipitation is expected across northern and western
Mainland Alaska while chances for enhanced precipitation increase to the
southeast, topping 40 percent in the southeastern Mainland and the Panhandle.
Building heights across Hawaii favors near normal precipitation in most
locations, with subnormal amounts nominally favored across Kauai, consistent
with a preponderance of the precipitation tools.
The official 8-14 day 500-hPa height blend consists of: 45% of Today's 6z GFS
Ensemble Mean centered on Day 11, 35% of Today's 0z European Ensemble Mean
centered on Day 11, and 20% of Today's 0z Canadian Ensemble Mean centered on
Day 11
FORECAST CONFIDENCE FOR THE 8-14 DAY PERIOD: Below average, 2 out of 5, due to
differences in how the models handle the orientation of 500-hPa positive height
 anomalies in northern North America, and how quickly mid-level heights drop in
the south-central and southwestern CONUS . In addition, temperature and
precipitation output from the ensembles is in fair agreement at best, and
inconsistencies continue between the raw and the statistically-adjusted
temperature and precipitation tools.
FORECASTER: Rich Tinker

week 3-4.text:
Prognostic Discussion for Week 3-4 Temperature and Precipitation Outlooks
 NWS Climate Prediction Center College Park MD
 300PM EST Fri Nov 20 2026
 Week 3-4 Forecast Discussion Valid Sat Dec 05 2026-Fri Dec 18 2026
 The Week 3–4 Outlook relies primarily on dynamical model guidance, complemented by analysis of tropical and extratropical teleconnections. El Niño conditions remain persistent in the tropics, characterized by weekly sea surface temperature (SST) anomalies reaching 2.2 °C in the Niño3.4 region, which is anticipated to influence both the Temperature and Precipitation Outlooks. Within the extratropics, recent dynamical guidance indicates a negative trend in the Arctic Oscillation (AO), likely linked to a Sudden Stratospheric Warming (SSW) event in mid-November. Although both teleconnections contribute to the atmospheric pattern, the El Niño signal serves as the primary driver for this forecast period.
 The large-scale circulation pattern shown in the manual blend of dynamical and statistical forecast tools reflects the extratropical teleconnection associated with El Niño. High-latitude anomalous ridging is indicated over Canada, while anomalous troughing extends from the North Pacific across the southern tier of the Contiguous United States (CONUS). This atmospheric pattern also resembles a negative AO-like signal, though the positive height anomalies are shifted further over Canada compared to their typical Arctic position. While dynamical and statistical models generally align well on this overall pattern, key differences remain. Model disagreement persists regarding the location of troughing over Alaska, especially in western regions, and models vary on the intensity of southern troughing, with the ECMWF projecting the weakest signal and the CFS predicting the strongest.
 The Week 3-4 Temperature Outlook favors above-normal temperatures across the western coastline and northern tier of the CONUS consistent with the El Nino signature in temperatures. Due to weak, inconsistent model signals and uncertainty regarding anomalous southern tier troughing across dynamical and statistical tools, Equal Chances (EC) of above-, near-, or below-normal temperatures are forecast for both the Southeast and Southern Plains. In Alaska, anomalous southerly flow drives above-normal temperatures, particularly in eastern parts of the state.
 Consistent with the previous week's forecast, the Week 3–4 Precipitation Outlook continues to indicate enhanced probabilities of above-normal precipitation throughout the southern tier. The highest probabilities are concentrated along the East Coast, driven by an extended subtropical jet and a southward shift of the mean climatological storm track characteristic of El Niño winters. Additionally, precipitation anomalies favor above-normal conditions stretching from the Pacific Northwest into the Alaska Panhandle promoted by anomalous onshore flow linked to troughing. Although dynamical models consistently project this atmospheric pattern, any westward adjustment of the trough would reduce both onshore flow and the anticipated precipitation anomalies. Conversely, below-normal precipitation is anticipated across the Northern Plains beneath the influence of anomalous ridging.
 The ongoing El Niño also continues to impact the Temperature and Precipitation Outlooks for Hawaii, where above-normal temperatures and below-normal precipitation probabilities are consistently favored by dynamical model guidance.
 Forecaster: Laura Ciasto
 The next week 3-4 outlook will be issued on Friday, Nov 27, 2026
 These outlooks are based on departures from the 1991-2020 base period
 These are three category outlooks consistent with what is currently used for the monthly and seasonal forecasts.
 The shading on the temperature map depicts the most favored category, either above-normal (A), below-normal (B), or near-normal (N) with the solid lines giving the probability ( >33%) of this more likely category (above, below, or near).
 The shading on the precipitation map depicts the most favored category, either above-median (A), below-median (B), or near-median with the solid lines giving the probability ( >33%) of this more likely category (above, below, or near).
 In areas where the likelihoods of 2-week mean temperatures and accumulated precipitation amounts are similar to climatological probabilities, equal chances (EC) is indicated.

Prognostic Discussion for Monthly Outlook NWS Climate Prediction Center College Park MD 300 PM EDT Sat Oct 31 2026 30-DAY OUTLOOK DISCUSSION FOR NOV 2026 The November 2026 Monthly Temperature and Precipitation Outlooks are updated considering monthly Climate Forecast System version 2 (CFSv2) temperature and precipitation forecasts, as well as information from an experimental monthly calibrated version of the Global Ensemble Forecast System (GEFSv12), and information from the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecast (ECMWF) model for the month of November. We also consider shorter term guidance and official Outlooks across the month, including days 1 to 7 precipitation, extended-range (6-10 Day and Week-2) tools and Outlooks, and subseasonal (Weeks 3-4) tools and Outlooks. The ongoing El Nino remains the dominant teleconnection to influence this forecast, overshadowing any potential impacts of the Madden-Julian Oscillation (MJO) despite an amplifying MJO signal that recently progressed eastward over the Indian Ocean basin, and the potential for continued eastward propagation in dynamical model forecasts. Adding to the uncertainty of this forecast, model forecasts indicate the potential for a stratospheric polar vortex disruption and a possible transition into a sudden stratospheric warming (SSW) next week. A November SSW is very rare, and should this occur, impacts can be seen for up to 2 months, usually manifesting as a negative Arctic Oscillation (AO) phase, which can already be seen in models. A negative AO is in contrast with the forecasted phase of the Pacific-North American (PNA) pattern, which is more in alignment with El Nino. These factors add some uncertainty to the eastern U.S., where some of the potential impacts of a SSW and negative AO compete with those from El Nino. Toward the early part of November, above-average heights are forecast across Canada and northern parts of the Contiguous United States (CONUS). Over the southern states, the pattern is more transient with weaker and progressive troughing forecast to move across the southern part of the CONUS. By mid-November, troughing off the West Coast is forecast to strengthen and move toward the coast, causing the ridging downstream to build and expand further southward and eastward. Late in the month, weeks 3-4 guidance favors persistence of the northern CONUS ridging. Troughing remains present off the West Coast of the US, and there is some potential for troughing to settle over the Southeast by the end of the month as well; however, models are uncertain on placement and strength. Overall, the beginning to middle of November is characterized by above average heights over the north, an active southern tier with progressive troughing, and below average heights to the west and east of the CONUS. By the end of November, the mid-level height pattern resembles a classic El Nino response. The pattern of strong troughing off the West Coast with ridging over Canada and northern parts of the CONUS leads to generally increasing 500 hPa height anomalies from south to north across Alaska by mid-to-late November, but the evolution becomes more uncertain as the month progresses. The updated November Temperature Outlook resembles the initial November Outlook in terms of the broad pattern of enhanced above-normal probabilities across the northern CONUS and along both coasts. However, there are some key changes in the updated Temperature Outlook, including expansion of above-normal temperatures across the state of Alaska, increased coverage of above-normal temperatures over the CONUS, reaching further south and covering more of the Southeast, and expansion of 50 to 60% probabilities of above-normal temperatures across the northern tier. The persistent ridging forecast throughout the month of November supports the increased coverage and strengthening of probabilities over the northern tier. Monthly CFSv2 forecasts depict high probabilities (greater than 75%) across Alaska, the northern CONUS, and the Southeast. However, probabilities are weaker in shorter-term tools, the experimental GEFSv12 and ECMWF, and the potential for cooler periods linked to the SSW and negative AO warrant lower probabilities than CFSv2. Transient guidance over the southern tier increases uncertainty early in the month, and equal-chances of above-, near-, and below-normal (EC) temperatures are indicated where guidance diverges the most. The potential late-month Southeast CONUS troughing reduces probabilities there, however, monthly guidance still agrees on a tilt toward above-normal temperatures. The highest confidence (60 to 70% chances) is located over the Northern Plains and Upper Mississippi Valley, aligned with persistent ridging and strong model agreement. While the updated Precipitation Outlook favors above-normal precipitation in that region which may lead to some cooling, this precipitation is expected to fall early in November. Though there is some uncertainty over western parts of Alaska, the pattern and above-average SSTs to the south generally support above-normal temperatures for the month. Larger changes were made to the updated November Precipitation Outlook to account for the potential for early-November precipitation across parts of the Southwest, Central and Northern Plains, and Upper Mississippi Valley. Since these regions are generally dry, it is much easier for short-lived early November precipitation to tilt the Outlook for the month to above-normal. Days 1 to 7 QPF indicates upper-tercile accumulations across parts of the Southwest and the Central and Northern Plains. Supported by monthly CFSv2, GEFSv12, and ECMWF guidance, above-normal precipitation probabilities are raised to 60% in the Southwest, with a 50% tilt across the north-central CONUS. Troughing off the Northwest Coast also supports a tilt toward above-normal precipitation along much of the West, including the Pacific Northwest, however, timing and amount of precipitation is uncertain. Conversely, probabilities are decreased across the Southeast and East Coast relative to the initial November Outlook. Most tools for the initial November Outlook favored a largely El Nino driven response over the Southeast and East Coast. However, the transient pattern for at least the first half of November increases uncertainty for the Southeast, and early November QPF forecasts are quite dry for much of the East and Southeast (except over peninsular Florida). In addition, Week 2 precipitation forecasts favor a weak below-normal precipitation probability that covers parts of the East and dips into the Southeast, also increasing uncertainty. Some moderate probability for above-normal precipitation remains over the Southeast given monthly dynamical model forecasts, but probabilities are weaker than the initial Outlook. Over Alaska, dynamical models had more agreement than in the initial Outlook and are in agreement with a typical El Nino response over the State. ****************************************************************************** ***** Previous mid-month discussion below ***** ****************************************************************************** The November 2026 Monthly Temperature and Precipitation Outlooks are based on dynamical models, local sea surface temperature (SST) anomalies, El Nino teleconnections, and decadal trends . Guidance incorporates individual models and multi-model ensembles (MME) from the Copernicus Climate System (C3S) and the North American Multi-Model Ensemble (NMME), alongside probability anomaly correlation (PAC) calibrated NMME forecasts and statistical tools blending SSTs and trends . Short-term early November forecasts from the Climate Forecast System version 2 (CFSv2), the Global Ensemble Forecast System version 12 (GEFSv12), and the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) models are utilized, along with monthly forecasts from CFSv2 and the experimental beta version of the Seasonal Forecast System (SFS) model. El Nino is expected to be the dominant climate driver, overshadowing the Madden-Julian Oscillation (MJO), though localized SST influences are possible. Dynamical model forecasts closely align with the expected El Nino teleconnection for November. However, short-term fluctuations in the pattern can occur, adding to uncertainty in some areas. Furthermore, while current El Nino conditions are forecast to strengthen, November can still be a transition month for ENSO impacts for some regions, with teleconnections strengthening through the winter months. The November 2026 Temperature Outlook depicts enhanced above-normal probabilities across the northern two-thirds of the Contiguous United States (CONUS) and along both coasts. Overall, models and tools favor a warmer northern tier of the CONUS, particularly over Washington and the interior Northwest, Northern Plains, Upper Mississippi Valley, and Great Lakes where probabilities are highest in the Outlook. Probabilities are damped over Oregon due to neutral SST anomalies . However, a southerly gradient toward above-average SSTs maintains a tilt toward above-normal along the West Coast. Probabilities are also weaker over Montana and North Dakota where diving troughs may introduce cooler spells. Inter-model spread increases uncertainty over New England and other areas where probabilities are comparatively lower. Equal chances (EC) of above-, near-, and below-normal temperatures are indicated over the Southwest to the Lower Mississippi Valley, including parts of the Central Plains and Intermountain West. While El Nino typically supports below-normal temperatures over the Southern Plains and Southwest, inconsistent model signals regarding the placement and strength of any below-normal temperatures prompt a tilt toward EC. For Alaska, enhanced probabilities transition from near-normal in the west to above-normal across the east, the southeast Mainland, and Southeast Alaska. Monthly models and tools and early November dynamical model forecasts are in very good agreement on above-normal temperatures over much of eastern Alaska, aligning with El Nino teleconnections, long-term temperature trends , and above-average coastal SSTs to the south. Western Alaska carries higher uncertainty, with most models showing weakening probabilities, EC, or isolated transitions toward below-normal temperatures. This results in an EC forecast for the remainder of the state, aside from a small NMME-based near-normal area on the west coast. The November 2026 Precipitation Outlook indicates enhanced above-normal probabilities across much of the southern US and the East Coast, with below-normal precipitation favored from the northern Intermountain West into parts of the Northern Plains, as well as parts of the Great Lakes. Model agreement is exceptionally high over the Southeast, with MMEs showing greater than 70% chances of above-normal precipitation in isolated areas. Accordingly, 60 to 70% probabilities are forecast for parts of the region. The above-normal precipitation extends up the East Coast, but increasing inter-model spread over New England supports a transition to EC. Similarly, disagreement regarding the northward extent of precipitation along the West Coast and central Plains results in EC designations, as location is difficult to pinpoint at this lead time amid high model spread . The western below-normal precipitation signal remains spatially consistent and aligns with El Nino, though some models expand it weakly toward the coast. However, uncertainty over the Pacific Northwest remains high enough to warrant EC along the coast. The eastern below-normal signal is most consistent over the Great Lakes, though some models like CFSv2 extend it further south toward the Gulf States. Over Alaska, a weak trend -based tilt toward below-normal precipitation covers the southwestern mainland and parts of the Aleutians, with elevated above-normal chances along the northern coast. EC is favored for the rest of the state due to weak, inconsistent model signals and November's status as an ENSO transition month before below-normal teleconnections become prevalent later in winter. FORECASTER: Johnna Infanti The climatic normals are based on conditions between 1991 and 2020, following the World Meteorological Organization convention of using the most recent 3 complete decades as the climate reference period.  The probability anomalies for temperature and precipitation based on these new normals better represent shorter term climatic anomalies than the forecasts based on older normals. Prognostic Discussion for Long-Lead Seasonal Outlooks NWS Climate Prediction Center College Park MD 830 AM EST Thu Nov 19 2026 SUMMARY OF THE OUTLOOK FOR NON-TECHNICAL USERS A strong El Nino continues and is forecast to persist through January-February-March 2027. The strong El Nino is likely to be the major influence on temperatures and precipitation this winter through next spring. The Temperature Outlook for December-January-February (DJF) 2026-2027 favors above-normal temperatures for central to eastern Alaska along with much of the northern two-thirds of the Contiguous U.S. (CONUS). Above-normal temperature probabilities exceed 50% across the Northeast, Great Lakes, Upper Mississippi Valley, Pacific Northwest, and southeastern Alaska. Near-normal temperatures, averaged over the three-month period, are favored for parts of the Southeast. The DJF Precipitation Outlook depicts an increased chance of above-normal precipitation for southwestern Oregon, California, the Southwest, Central to Southern Great Plains, Southeast, Mid-Atlantic, and much of the Northeast. The largest above-normal precipitation probabilities (> 70% chance) are forecast across Florida, southern Georgia, and the coastal Carolinas. Below-normal precipitation is more likely for parts of the Great Lakes, Northern High Plains, Northern Rockies, and Mainland Alaska. Equal chances (EC, white areas) are forecast for areas where probabilities for each category (below, near, or above) of three-month mean temperatures and accumulated precipitation amounts are forecast to be similar to climatological probabilities. BASIS AND SUMMARY OF THE CURRENT LONG-LEAD OUTLOOKS Note: For Graphical Displays of the Forecast Tools Discussed Below See: http://www. cpc .ncep.noaa.gov/products/predictions/90day/tools/briefing CURRENT ATMOSPHERIC AND OCEANIC CONDITIONS As of mid-November, weekly observed sea surface temperature (SST) departures in the Nino 3.4 region are +2.2 degrees C with equatorial SSTs above average across the east-central Pacific Ocean. Upper-ocean (0 to 300 meters) anomalies from the Date Line to 100W are near +2.5 degrees C but have decreased slightly since peaking in September. The Relative Oceanic Nino Index for August-September-October was +2.0 degrees C, just shy of +2.1 degrees C in 1997. From mid-October to mid-November, below-average OLR anomalies (enhanced convection and precipitation) were observed across the east-central equatorial Pacific with above-average OLR anomalies (suppressed convection and precipitation) across Indonesia and the Maritime Continent. Low-level and upper-level (850-hPa and 200-hPa) wind anomalies were westerly and easterly, respectively, from 160E to 120W. The oceanic and atmospheric observations reflect an ongoing strong El Nino. Any Madden-Julian Oscillation (MJO) signal continues to be overwhelmed and masked by the strong El Nino. Upper-level velocity potential anomaly observations depict a MJO that propagated east to the Indian Ocean by mid-November. Dynamical model forecasts indicate that this MJO may propagate east to the Western Hemisphere by the beginning of December. However, the MJO is unlikely to have much influence on the mid-latitude circulation pattern given the strength of the El Nino. PROGNOSTIC DISCUSSION OF SST FORECASTS As of November 12, the NOAA outlook indicates that El Nino is likely to persist through MAM 2027 with a transition to ENSO-neutral conditions becoming more probable by AMJ. The SST consolidation forecast for Nino 3.4 depicts SST anomalies peaking above +2.5 degrees C during NDJ 2026-27 and decreasing later in the winter and into the spring. By the 2027 fall and 2027-28 winter, this prognostic tool depicts a weak to moderate La Nina with SST anomalies between -0.5 and -1.0 degrees C. PROGNOSTIC TOOLS USED FOR U.S. TEMPERATURE AND PRECIPITATION OUTLOOKS The Temperature and Precipitation Outlooks from DJF 2026-27 through AMJ 2027 were based on: dynamical models such as the North American Multi-Model Ensemble (NMME) and the International Multi-Model Ensemble (IMME) along with an objective, historical skill-weighted consolidation that includes the NMME along with statistical tools such as the SST-based Constructed Analog and the ENSO-OCN. Also, for DJF 2026-27, observed temperatures and precipitation during stronger El Ninos (since 1997-98) and strong/very strong El Nino composites were heavily weighed. Beginning in MJJ and through OND 2027, ENSO-OCN (combination of ENSO and long-term trend) was the primary tool used. During NDJ and DJF 2027-28, the outlooks incorporated La Nina composites. PROGNOSTIC DISCUSSION OF OUTLOOKS - DJF 2026 TO DJF 2027 TEMPERATURE The historically strong El Nino is forecast to be the major influence on the mid-latitude circulation pattern and temperatures this winter. Typically during El Nino winters, DJF temperatures average above normal for most of the northern two-thirds of the CONUS with three-month temperatures more variable and averaging either below, near, or above normal for the southern third of the CONUS. The DJF 2026-27 outlook closely followed El Nino composites and the latest dynamical model output (NMME and IMME). Above-normal temperature probabilities exceed 50% for much of the Northeast, Great Lakes, Upper Mississippi Valley, Pacific Northwest, and southeastern Alaska. In addition, these probabilities are largest (> 60%) from northwestern Oregon and Washington northward to southeastern Alaska due to the latest dynamical model output and strong/very strong El Nino composites. Forecast uncertainty is higher for the Southwest, Southern Great Plains, Gulf Coast, and Southeast during the 2026-27 winter through the 2027 spring. Without a major shift in any of the model guidance, no changes were made to these areas from the previous outlook. In the more recent stronger El Ninos (2023-24, 2015-16, and 1997-98), temperatures varied largely over the Southwest where equal chances (EC) of below, near, or above-normal temperature are forecast. During the 2023-24 and 1997-98 winters, DJF temperatures verified in the middle tercile for most of Florida and from southeastern Louisiana east to southern Georgia. Therefore, the DJF 2026-27 temperature outlook leans towards near normal temperatures being the most likely outcome for that part of the Southeast. The DJF temperature observations for 2009-10 (stronger El Nino) was heavily influenced by a persistent and highly negative Arctic Oscillation (AO) with the following monthly values: Dec: -3.4, Jan: -2.6, Feb: -4.3. Although the 2009-10 winter outcome with a broad coverage of below-normal temperatures across the Great Plains and Southeast can not be completely ruled out, it is the least likely one among the more recent stronger El Ninos. The primary source of uncertainty in the temperature outlook is how much high latitude blocking prevails this winter. The AO and North Atlantic Oscillation (NAO) was in a positive phase from mid-September through October, but became negative in early November. The GEFS and ECMWF ensemble means favor a -NAO heading into December. A -NAO would tend to result in below-normal temperatures across the Southeast but there is high uncertainty on the NAO phase through the 2026-27 winter. El Nino impacts are expected to persist through at least the spring 2027 and the temperature outlooks reflect this. The outlooks from MJJ through OND 2027 are based primarily on the ENSO-OCN forecast tool which is derived from the CPC SST consolidation (ENSO component) and long term temperature trends (Optimal Climate Normal). Historically, La Nina follows a strong El Nino and given this likelihood, the NDJ and DJF 2027-28 outlooks were based more on typical La Nina influences. PRECIPITATION Due to the historically strong El Nino and its reliable wet pattern for a majority of the CONUS, there is higher forecast confidence in the precipitation than the temperature outlook this winter. For DJF 2026-27, a predicted active southern stream along with enhanced subtropical moisture leads to a large coverage of greater than a 40% chance of above-normal precipitation from southwestern Oregon and California east through the Southwest, Central to Southern Great Plains, Gulf Coast, and much of the East Coast. Based on the latest dynamical model output, above-normal precipitation probabilities were increased across California, the Desert Southwest, and along the East Coast compared to the previous forecast release on October 15. In southern California and southwestern Arizona, probabilities exceed 60% while greater than a 70% chance of above-normal precipitation is forecast for Florida, southern Georgia, and the coastal Carolinas. The elevated above-normal precipitation probabilties extend north to the western Corn Belt and also along the West Coast to Oregon given the good model agreement and strong/very strong El Nino composites. Excellent model consistency the past few months along with strong/very strong El Nino composites support below-normal precipitation probabilities exceeding 50% across the northern Rockies and much of Mainland Alaska. Consistent with the El Nino response and its southward shift in the storm track, elevated below-normal precipitation probabilities are forecast for parts of the Great Lakes and Northern Great Plains. The Pacific Decadal Oscillation (PDO) has remained negative throughout the 2020s. Although the October 2026 PDO value was negative, positive SST anomalies have diminished over the northeastern Pacific due to fall storminess. It is uncertain if the -PDO persists through the 2026-27 winter, and regardless, it is likely that the historically strong El Nino will be the major influence on the precipitation pattern across the Lower 48 states. El Nino impacts typically peak during the late winter across the Southeast, which supports maintaining large above-normal precipitation probabilities (> 70%) for that region through JFM. Since El Nino impacts are expected to linger into the spring, there is greater than a 40% chance of above-normal precipitation across much of California along with parts of the Southwest and Southeast during FMA and MAM. The precipitation outlooks from MJJ through OND 2027 are based on the ENSO-OCN forecast tool which is from the CPC SST consolidation (ENSO component) and long term temperature trends (Optimal Climate Normal). Historically, La Nina follows a strong El Nino and given this likelihood, the NDJ and DJF 2027-28 outlooks were based more on La Nina influences. FORECASTER: Brad Pugh The Climatic normals are based on conditions between 1991 and 2020, following the World Meterological Organization convention of using the most recent 3 complete decades as the climatic reference period.  The probability anomalies for temperature and precipitation based on these new normals better represent shorter term climatic anomalies than the forecasts based on older normals.
